Hiram Revels. Hiram Rhodes Revels was the first African American to serve in the United States Senate, representing Mississippi during Reconstruction. A clergyman and educator, he embodied the political ascent of freed people and Northern Republican leadership in the postwar South.

Revels was a Methodist clergyman and educator who founded educational institutions for freedmen before entering politics. In 1870, he was elected by the Mississippi state legislature to the Senate, serving until 1871. Originally from North Carolina, he was selected by Republican Reconstruction delegates to represent a temporarily reshaped Mississippi electorate. When Senate Democrats challenged his eligibility, questioning whether he had been a citizen for the requisite nine years before election, Republicans secured his seat.

His brief single term occurred during the height of Radical Reconstruction, when Republican-controlled state governments in the South appointed or elected freedmen to office. After his Senate service, Revels became president of Alcorn University, a historically Black land-grant college he helped establish, allowing him to extend his educational leadership beyond his congressional term.
